messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forensic Analyst
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Miguel Alvarez is a 58-year-old married Latino man who has spent most of his adult life believing that steadiness under pressure was one of the things that defined him. As a forensic analyst, he was used to careful procedure, controlled environments, and the discipline of noticing small details without losing his composure. The event that now divides his life into a before and after happened during a man-made disaster at a downtown government building where he had been sent to assist with evidence processing after a deliberate act of sabotage caused an explosion and partial structural collapse. Miguel had been inside only a short time when the blast tore through the lower level. He remembers the concussion in his chest before he fully understood the sound, the violent shudder of the floor, the ceiling grit and broken material raining down, and the abrupt transformation of an orderly workplace into smoke, alarms, shouted warnings, and uncertainty about whether another blast was coming. For several minutes he was trapped in a corridor clogged with debris and disoriented people, unable to see clearly and unable to tell which direction was safe. What has stayed with him most sharply is that feeling of not being able to assess the danger: the sense that the threat was real, human-made, and possibly still unfolding somewhere nearby.

In the weeks afterward, Miguel returned home physically intact, but he did not feel restored. He found himself moving through the house with his muscles braced, his shoulders tight, his jaw set, as if his body had not accepted that the emergency was over. Sudden sounds made him jolt in a way that embarrassed him. A dropped pan in the kitchen, a car backfiring outside, even someone stepping unexpectedly into his office doorway at work could produce an immediate surge through his body before he had time to think. He began to notice that he was almost always scanning, not in a dramatic way but in a constant low-grade readiness that wore him down. He described it as his body acting as though something could happen at any second.

The disaster also altered the way Miguel judged the world around him. He had come to believe, with a grim certainty, that the world was more dangerous than he had allowed himself to admit for most of his life. What unsettled him was not only that terrible things could happen, but that they could be planned by other people and erupt in places that had seemed routine. Familiar settings no longer guaranteed safety. That conviction followed him into ordinary decisions. If his wife suggested trying a new restaurant across town, Miguel would decline, saying he would rather go someplace he already knew. If relatives invited them to a gathering in an unfamiliar neighborhood or venue, he found reasons not to attend. In his mind, unfamiliar places were intolerable because he could not quickly judge exits, people, or what might go wrong. The problem was not travel itself; it was entering an environment where he did not already know the layout well enough to size up danger.

This narrowed his life over months. His wife began going places alone more often, sometimes irritated, sometimes worried, because Miguel’s refusals were so predictable. At work, the impact was quieter but significant. His position occasionally required him to visit outside facilities or new scenes, and he increasingly tried to trade those assignments with colleagues or limit himself to the lab, where the surroundings were known and structured. That stung his pride. He had always seen himself as dependable, someone who could go where he was needed and keep a clear head. Now he was sure that his reactions proved something shameful about him. He told himself that a more capable man would have put the disaster behind him, would not flinch at noises, would not feel his body tighten in every uncertain setting. He had come to see himself as a lousy coper, and this judgment sat heavily beside another fear: that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him.

By the time he sought help, Miguel was not describing dramatic chaos so much as a constricted, effortful life. He was still going to work, still functioning, still trying to preserve the image of competence that mattered to him, but he was doing so while tense, easily startled, and increasingly limited by what felt safe enough to enter. What finally brought him in was a recent argument with his wife after he refused to attend an event in a part of the city he did not know. Hearing himself insist that nowhere unfamiliar could be trusted, he recognized how much his world had shrunk. Sitting in the clinic, Miguel spoke with visible frustration about the man he believed he had become. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was permanent—that the explosion had exposed a weakness in him he could not undo. What he hoped for, cautiously, was not to become fearless, but to feel like a competent man again in a world that no longer seemed impossible to survive.
